abstract: The Centre for British Progress published a comprehensive analysis of AI's impact on the UK labour market three years after generative AI reached the market, authored by Dr Pedro Serôdio. The central finding is that there is no detectable employment effect for the most AI-exposed occupations in UK data, regardless of which exposure metric is used — the estimates are noisy, confidence intervals are wide, and neither measure produces a statistically distinguishable effect on aggregate employment. The analysis examines 412 occupations using four distinct exposure metrics: the ILO task-based index, the Eloundou et al. GPT-4 assessment, Anthropic's revealed adoption measure, and the Massenkoff & McCrory observed exposure metric. Results hold consistently across all four. Occupations with high AI exposure actually experienced marginally faster cumulative employment growth since ChatGPT's launch. UK workers use AI across 385 distinct work tasks (2.1% of the O*NET database), with the top fifth of tasks accounting for 63% of UK activity. AI autonomy remains flat at approximately 3.4/5 across adoption levels, showing no trend toward independent operation. High-exposure occupations show slower wage growth, but this divergence predates ChatGPT by 2-3 years and cannot be attributed to AI. In the software sector specifically, GVA per worker accelerated from 0.8% annually pre-ChatGPT to 3.8% post-launch, while programmer vacancy rates fell sharply to one-third of pre-pandemic levels.
keyFindings: No detectable employment effect for the most AI-exposed occupations in UK data three years after generative AI's arrival, regardless of which exposure metric is used.
High-exposure occupations show slower wage growth than low-exposure ones, but this divergence predates ChatGPT by 2-3 years, indicating structural rather than AI-driven causes.
Predicted exposure indices generally overstate realized adoption — more occupations adopt less AI than predictions suggest, with professional/managerial roles showing the widest gap.
Software sector productivity (GVA per worker) accelerated from 0.8% to 3.8% annually post-ChatGPT, while programmer vacancy rates fell to one-third of pre-pandemic levels.
AI autonomy remains flat at ~3.4/5 across all adoption levels, showing no trend toward independent operation — usage is augmentation-dominant with automation rare.
methodology: Statistical analysis of 412 occupations using the Annual Population Survey/Labour Force Survey (2004-2025), Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings (payroll-based wage and hours data), Anthropic Economic Index (millions of real conversations mapped to O*NET tasks), and ONS sectoral output data. Four distinct AI exposure metrics applied: ILO task-based index, Eloundou et al. (2023) GPT-4 assessment, Anthropic revealed adoption, and Massenkoff & McCrory (2026) observed exposure. Employment effects assessed through difference-in-differences style analysis with wide confidence intervals reported.
qualifiers: UK data is hampered by a 2021 occupational classification break that limits panel length. Post-COVID recovery dynamics confound growth trends, making it difficult to isolate AI effects. Survey-based labour market data updates less frequently than technology deployment. The analysis cannot capture task-level reallocation or within-occupation shifts that might precede employment-level effects. UK has lower per-worker AI adoption intensity than the US, limiting generalizability of null findings. The report explicitly notes these results do not rule out larger future effects but constrain near-term predictions to actual adoption patterns.
